questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-5t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(-5t)={e}^{-5t} \\ r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}-5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-5t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-10t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot (-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} \\ {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(-4t)={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t)={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix
questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by substitution from $\text{L1}.$
